title: Strang concedes it would be a mere war of words (De voluntate Dei III.14, p. 687)
source_text: XIII. Et revera inter eos qui docent libertatem in genere oppositam esse non necessitati sed coactioni, id diserte affirmat Strangius Scholae Reformatae Doctor. Postquam enim multis docuit voluntatem liberam esse non tantum quum versatur circa media, sed etiam quum versatur circa finem, ac proinde Deum libere se amare, & homines libere velle esse foelices, quia libertas voluntatis in genere non est aliud quam spontaneum intellectuale: Et postea fassus est libertatem strictius etiam usurpari, prout versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & restringitur ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, quo respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, & actus liberi sunt mere contingentes; Deinde quoque observavit in hoc sensu a multis negari quod Deus libere se amet, & beati in coelo libere Deum diligant, concludit tandem his verbis, Neque nobis videtur hac de re litigandum, quia alioqui tantum esset λογομαχία, non enim negamus, sic vocem liberi arbitrii recte usurpari, quanquam in alio sensu illas actiones diximus esse liberas. De voluntate Dei lib. 3. cap. 14. pag. 687.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed among those who teach that liberty in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, Strang a Doctor of the Reformed School expressly affirms this. For after he had taught at length that the will is free not only when it is concerned with means, but also when it is concerned with the end, and accordingly that God loves himself freely, and men freely will to be happy, because the liberty of the will in general is nothing else than the intellectual spontaneous: And afterwards had confessed that liberty is used also more strictly, as it is concerned with τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, that is, those things which are in our power, and is restricted to means related to the end, or to those which conduce little, or nothing to the end, in which respect liberty includes a certain indifference, and free acts are merely contingent; Then also had observed that in this sense it is denied by many that God freely loves himself, and that the blessed in heaven freely love God, he concludes at length in these words, Nor does it seem to us that we must contend about this matter, because otherwise it would be only a logomachy, for we do not deny, that the word free choice is rightly used thus, although in another sense we have said those actions are free. On the will of God book 3. chap. 14. page 687.
pass_b_english: Among those who teach that freedom in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, the Reformed teacher John Strang says this in so many words. He first argued at length that the will is free not only in dealing with means but also in dealing with the end, so that God loves himself freely and men freely will to be happy, since freedom of the will in general is nothing but intellectual spontaneity.

He then admitted that freedom is also used in a narrower sense, for what concerns τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, the things in our power, and limited to means ordered to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to the end. In that respect freedom includes a certain indifference, and free acts are purely contingent. He further noted that many deny, in this sense, that God loves himself freely or that the blessed in heaven love God freely.

He finally concludes: 'We do not think this matter worth a quarrel, since it would otherwise be a mere war of words (λογομαχία). For we do not deny that the term free choice is properly used in that way, although in another sense we have called those actions free.' (De voluntate Dei, book 3, chapter 14, page 687.)

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
